title: Stoicism
brief: Explain in simple words what Stoicism is and convince teachers it's worth discussing with students.
quirk: Isn't Stoicism just about suppressing your emotions?
trick: Isn't Stoicism just about suppressing your emotions?
summary: Stoicism is a philosophical movement and practical guide to living, emphasizing daily self-discipline and moral improvement, which originated in the Hellenistic period of ancient Greece and continued well into the Roman Imperial period.

title: Utilitarianism
brief: Explain the idea of "the greatest good for the greatest number" and convince the jury it helps people make decisions.
quirk: So it's fine to sacrifice one person to save five?
trick: So it's fine to sacrifice one person to save five?
summary: Utilitarianism is a family of theories in normative ethics that prescribe actions that maximize happiness and well-being for all affected individuals. In other words, utilitarian ideas encourage actions that lead to the greatest good for the greatest number.

title: Existentialism
brief: Explain what "existence precedes essence" means and convince ordinary people that this idea brings freedom, not despair.
quirk: If life has no given meaning, why do anything at all?
trick: If life has no given meaning, why do anything at all?
summary: Existentialism is a family of philosophical views and inquiry that explore the human individual's struggle to lead an authentic life despite the apparent absurdity or incomprehensibility of existence.

title: Ikigai
brief: Explain the Japanese idea of ikigai and convince business people it helps keep employees.
quirk: Isn't the four-circle diagram a Western invention rather than a Japanese tradition?
trick: Isn't the four-circle diagram a Western invention rather than a Japanese tradition?
summary: Ikigai  is a Japanese concept of an individual's definition of the meaning of their life.

sources.title: BBC Worklife: Ikigai — a Japanese concept to improve work and life

title: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
brief: Explain why beginners overestimate themselves and convince teachers to take this into account when grading.
quirk: Some say this effect is just a statistical artifact. Does it even exist?
trick: Some say this effect is just a statistical artifact. Does it even exist?
summary: The Dunning–Kruger effect is a cognitive bias that describes the systematic tendency of people with low ability in a specific area to give overly positive assessments of their ability. The term may also refer to the tendency of high performers to underestimate their skills.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Dunning–Kruger effect (easy English)

title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
brief: Explain the sunk cost trap with an example and convince business people to shut down failing projects in time.
quirk: Isn't persistence the most important quality of an entrepreneur?
trick: Isn't persistence the most important quality of an entrepreneur?
summary: In economics and business decision-making, a sunk cost is a cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered. Sunk costs are contrasted with prospective costs, which are future costs that may be avoided if action is taken.

title: Confirmation Bias
brief: Explain why we only notice what we already believe and convince people to fact-check the news.
quirk: How do you know you're not the biased one right now?
trick: How do you know you're not the biased one right now?
summary: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favor and recall information in a way that confirms or supports one's prior beliefs, values, or decisions.

title: Impostor Syndrome
brief: Explain what impostor syndrome is and convince the jury we need to talk about it openly.
quirk: What if the person really isn't good enough and we just call it a syndrome?
trick: What if the person really isn't good enough and we just call it a syndrome?
summary: Impostor syndrome, also known as impostor phenomenon, impostorism, or impostor thoughts, is a psychological experience in which a person suffers from feelings of intellectual and/or professional fraudulence.

title: First Principles Thinking
brief: Explain how to break a problem down to basic facts and convince business people to think this way instead of copying competitors.
quirk: That takes forever — why reinvent the wheel?
trick: That takes forever — why reinvent the wheel?
summary: In philosophy and science, a first principle is a basic proposition or assumption that cannot be deduced from any other proposition or assumption. First principles in philosophy are from first cause attitudes and taught by Aristotelians, and nuanced versions of first principles are referred to as postulates by Kantians.

title: Occam's Razor
brief: Explain the principle "don't multiply entities beyond necessity" and convince teachers to teach it to students.
quirk: The world is complex — isn't the simplest explanation often wrong?
trick: The world is complex — isn't the simplest explanation often wrong?
summary: In philosophy, Occam's razor is the problem-solving principle that recommends searching for explanations constructed with the smallest possible set of elements. It is also known as the principle of parsimony or the law of parsimony.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Occam's razor (easy English)

title: The Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)
brief: Explain the 80/20 rule with everyday examples and convince people to apply it to their own lives.
quirk: Why exactly 80 and 20 — is it a law of nature or just curve-fitting?
trick: Why exactly 80 and 20 — is it a law of nature or just curve-fitting?
summary: The Pareto principle states that, for many outcomes, roughly 80% of consequences come from 20% of causes.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Pareto principle (easy English)

title: Hanlon's Razor
brief: Explain the rule "never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by stupidity" and convince the jury it reduces conflict.
quirk: And what if someone really is acting with bad intentions?
trick: And what if someone really is acting with bad intentions?
summary: Hanlon's razor is an adage or rule of thumb that states, "Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity." It is a philosophical razor that promotes a way of eliminating unlikely explanations for human behavior, purportedly named after the American writer Robert J.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Hanlon's razor (easy English)

title: Opportunity Cost
brief: Explain that every choice has a hidden price and convince people to consider it when shopping or choosing a job.
quirk: If you keep counting what you missed, how can you ever enjoy your choice?
trick: If you keep counting what you missed, how can you ever enjoy your choice?
summary: In microeconomic theory, the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative forgone where, given limited resources, a choice needs to be made between several mutually exclusive alternatives.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Opportunity cost (easy English)

title: Inflation
brief: Explain why money loses value and convince teachers to teach financial literacy from school age.
quirk: Why should kids learn this if they don't have their own money yet?
trick: Why should kids learn this if they don't have their own money yet?
summary: In economics, inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money, though it originally referred to the increase of the money supply that can cause such a universal shift. This increase is measured using a price index, typically a consumer price index (CPI).

title: The Tragedy of the Commons
brief: Explain why shared resources get depleted and propose to the jury how to stop it.
quirk: Elinor Ostrom showed communities can manage shared resources. So is there even a problem?
trick: Elinor Ostrom showed communities can manage shared resources. So is there even a problem?
summary: The tragedy of the commons is the idea that when a resource is shared and can benefit the individual at a cost to the community, it is rational for the individual to overuse the resource, even though this collectively leads to the depletion of the resource for everyone.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Tragedy of the commons (easy English)

title: Universal Basic Income
brief: Explain the idea of universal basic income, take a side for or against, and convince business people.
quirk: Who will work if money is given away for free?
trick: Who will work if money is given away for free?
summary: Universal basic income (UBI) is a social welfare proposal in which all members of a given population regularly receive a minimum income in the form of an unconditional transfer payment, i.e., without a means test or need to perform work.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Basic income (easy English)

title: CRISPR Gene Editing
brief: Explain how CRISPR "cuts" genes and convince people it's an opportunity, not a threat.
quirk: What if people start making "designer babies"?
trick: What if people start making "designer babies"?
summary: CRISPR is a family of DNA sequences found in the genomes of prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria and archaea. Each sequence within an individual prokaryotic CRISPR is derived from a DNA fragment of a bacteriophage that had previously infected the prokaryote or one of its ancestors.

title: Herd Immunity
brief: Explain how one person's vaccination protects others and convince teachers to tell children about it.
quirk: If almost everyone around me is vaccinated, why should I get vaccinated?
trick: If almost everyone around me is vaccinated, why should I get vaccinated?
summary: Herd immunity is a form of indirect protection that applies only to contagious diseases.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Herd immunity (easy English)

title: Quantum Computing
brief: Explain in simple words how a quantum computer differs from a regular one and convince business people to keep an eye on this technology.
quirk: They've been promised for 20 years — isn't it always "ten years away"?
trick: They've been promised for 20 years — isn't it always "ten years away"?
summary: A quantum computer is a computer that represents and processes information using quantum states. Quantum computations exploit phenomena such as superposition, interference, and entanglement. Quantum computers have the potential to complete some calculations exponentially faster than classical computers.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Quantum computer (easy English)

title: The Human Microbiome
brief: Explain how the bacteria inside us affect health and mood and convince the jury it's one of the biggest discoveries in medicine.
quirk: Aren't these big claims based mostly on studies in mice?
trick: Aren't these big claims based mostly on studies in mice?
summary: The human microbiome is the aggregate of all microbiota that reside on or within human tissues and biofluids along with the corresponding anatomical sites in which they reside, including the gastrointestinal tract, skin, mammary glands, seminal fluid, uterus, ovarian follicles, lung, saliva, oral mucosa, ocular surface, and the biliary tract.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Human microbiome (easy English)

title: The Fermi Paradox
brief: Explain why we still haven't met aliens and convince the audience of your answer.
quirk: Maybe we're just not looking hard enough?
trick: Maybe we're just not looking hard enough?
summary: The Fermi paradox is the seeming inconsistency between the lack of evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the apparently high likelihood of their existence.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Fermi paradox (easy English)

title: Black Holes
brief: Explain what a black hole is without formulas and convince teachers it's worth discussing at school.
quirk: How can you study something you can't see?
trick: How can you study something you can't see?
summary: A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping. Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, which describes gravitation as the curvature of spacetime, predicts that any sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Black hole (easy English)

title: Terraforming Mars
brief: Explain how Mars could be made habitable and convince business people it's worth investing in now.
quirk: Wouldn't it be easier to save Earth than to build a second one?
trick: Wouldn't it be easier to save Earth than to build a second one?
summary: The terraforming of Mars is a hypothetical procedure that would consist of a planetary engineering project or concurrent projects aspiring to transform Mars from a planet hostile to life to one that could sustainably host humans and other lifeforms free of protection or mediation.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Terraforming of Mars (easy English)

title: Space Debris and the Kessler Syndrome
brief: Explain how debris in orbit could trap us on Earth and propose a solution to the jury.
quirk: Space is huge — why does it matter how much junk is up there?
trick: Space is huge — why does it matter how much junk is up there?
summary: The Kessler syndrome, also known as the Kessler effect, collisional cascading, or ablation cascade, is a scenario proposed by NASA scientists Donald J. Kessler and Burton G. Cour-Palais in 1978.

title: The Turing Test
brief: Explain what the Turing test is and convince teachers whether modern chatbots have passed it.
quirk: If a bot passes the test, does that mean it thinks?
trick: If a bot passes the test, does that mean it thinks?
summary: The Turing test was designed by Alan Turing to assess a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behaviour equivalent to that of a human by imitating interactive dialogue. In the modern version, a human evaluator judges a text transcript of a natural-language conversation between a human and a machine.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Turing test (easy English)

title: Large Language Models
brief: Explain how ChatGPT "predicts" the next word and convince people to use it wisely.
quirk: If it just predicts words, why should we trust it?
trick: If it just predicts words, why should we trust it?
summary: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a vast amount of text for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation. LLMs can typically generate, summarize, translate, and analyze text in many contexts.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Large language model (easy English)

title: The Technological Singularity
brief: Explain the idea of the singularity and convince the jury that it's near — or that it's a myth.
quirk: Is this science or science fiction?
trick: Is this science or science fiction?
summary: The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization. According to the most popular version of the singularity hypothesis, I. J.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Technological singularity (easy English)

title: Deepfakes
brief: Explain how deepfakes are made and convince business people to protect their company from them.
quirk: Can't we just ban deepfakes by law?
trick: Can't we just ban deepfakes by law?
summary: Deepfakes are images, videos, or audio that have been edited or generated using artificial intelligence, AI-based tools or audio-video editing software.

title: Growth Mindset
brief: Explain the difference between a fixed and a growth mindset and convince teachers to praise effort, not talent.
quirk: Recent studies show a small effect — isn't it just a motivational slogan?
trick: Recent studies show a small effect — isn't it just a motivational slogan?
summary: A mindset refers to an established set of attitudes of a person or group concerning culture, values, philosophy, frame of reference, outlook, or disposition. Person A is said to have a theory of mind (ToM) about person B, relating mindset research to ToM.

title: Flow State
brief: Explain what a flow state is and convince business people to organize work so employees can reach it.
quirk: Artists get into flow, but how do you get there in accounting?
trick: Artists get into flow, but how do you get there in accounting?
summary: Flow in positive psychology, also known colloquially as being in the zone or focused, is the mental state in which a person performing some activity is fully immersed in a feeling of energized focus, full involvement, and enjoyment in the process of the activity.

title: The Placebo Effect
brief: Explain why a "sugar pill" can heal and convince people it shows the power of the brain, not a trick.
quirk: Then why do we need real medicine at all?
trick: Then why do we need real medicine at all?
summary: A placebo is a medicine or treatment intended to appear genuine to its recipient, but which has no pharmaceutical effect. Common placebos include inert tablets, inert injections, sham surgery, and other procedures.

title: Procrastination
brief: Explain why we procrastinate and convince the jury it's an emotional problem, not laziness.
quirk: Maybe it really is just laziness and you need to pull yourself together?
trick: Maybe it really is just laziness and you need to pull yourself together?
summary: Procrastination is an avoidance coping behavior that involves unnecessarily delaying or postponing something despite knowing that there could be negative consequences for doing so.

title: The Four-Day Work Week
brief: Convince business people to switch to a four-day work week — or prove that it's a mistake.
quirk: Who will answer customers on Fridays?
trick: Who will answer customers on Fridays?
summary: A four-day workweek is an arrangement where a workplace or place of education has its employees or students work or attend school, college or university over the course of four days per week rather than the more customary five-day workweek.

sources.title: 4 Day Week Global — advocates of the 4-day week

title: Filter Bubbles
brief: Explain how algorithms lock us into a bubble of opinions and convince people to break out of it.
quirk: What's wrong with my feed showing me what I'm interested in?
trick: What's wrong with my feed showing me what I'm interested in?
summary: A filter bubble is a state of intellectual isolation that arises when personalized searches, recommendation systems, and algorithmic curation selectively presents information to each user; the search results are based on information about the user, such as their location, past click-behavior, and search history.

sources.title: TED: Eli Pariser — Beware online filter bubbles (9 min)
Farnam Street: How Filter Bubbles Distort Reality

title: Effective Altruism
brief: Explain how to help others "smartly" using data and convince the jury that charity should be effective.
quirk: Can you really measure other people's suffering in numbers?
trick: Can you really measure other people's suffering in numbers?
summary: Effective altruism (EA) is a 21st-century philosophical and social movement that advocates impartially calculating benefits and prioritizing causes to provide the greatest good.

title: Minimalism
brief: Explain the idea of "fewer things, more life" and convince teachers it's worth teaching young people.
quirk: Isn't minimalism just an expensive style for people who already have everything?
trick: Isn't minimalism just an expensive style for people who already have everything?
summary: Simple living refers to practices that promote simplicity in one's lifestyle. Common practices of simple living include reducing the number of possessions one owns, depending less on technology and services, ascetism, and spending less money.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Simple living (easy English)

title: Wabi-Sabi
brief: Explain the Japanese beauty of imperfection and convince people to stop chasing perfection.
quirk: Isn't that just an excuse for sloppy work?
trick: Isn't that just an excuse for sloppy work?
summary: In traditional Japanese aesthetics, wabi-sabi (侘び寂び) centers on the acceptance of transience and imperfection. It is often described as the appreciation of beauty that is "imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete". It is prevalent in many forms of Japanese art.

title: The Hero's Journey
brief: Explain the hero's journey structure and convince business people to build ads and pitches around it.
quirk: If every story follows the same template, isn't that boring?
trick: If every story follows the same template, isn't that boring?
summary: In narratology and comparative mythology, the hero's quest or hero's journey, also known as the monomyth, is the common template of stories that involve a hero who goes on an adventure, is victorious in a decisive crisis, and comes home changed or transformed.

sources.title: MasterClass: What Is the Hero's Journey?

title: The Golden Ratio
brief: Explain what the golden ratio is and convince teachers where it really appears and where it's a myth.
quirk: Isn't "the golden ratio in the Parthenon" just fitting the data to the answer?
trick: Isn't "the golden ratio in the Parthenon" just fitting the data to the answer?
summary:
In mathematics, two quantities are in the golden ratio if their ratio is the same as the ratio of their sum to the larger of the two quantities. Expressed algebraically, for quantities ⁠⁠ and ⁠⁠ with ⁠⁠, ⁠⁠ is in a golden ratio to ⁠⁠ if

where the Greek letter phi denotes the golden ratio.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Golden ratio (easy English)

title: Bauhaus
brief: Explain the principle "form follows function" and convince the jury that Bauhaus still shapes the design around us.
quirk: Didn't this style make cities gray and all the same?
trick: Didn't this style make cities gray and all the same?
summary: The Staatliches Bauhaus, commonly known as the Bauhaus, was a German art school operational from 1919 to 1933 that combined crafts and the fine arts. The school became famous for its approach to design, which attempted to unify individual artistic vision with the principles of mass production and emphasis on function.

title: The Printing Press
brief: Explain how the printing press changed the world and convince people the internet is its continuation.
quirk: The printing press spread lies too — isn't it the same with the internet?
trick: The printing press spread lies too — isn't it the same with the internet?
summary: A printing press is a machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto a surface made of paper, cloth, or a similar material. Its workers are known as printing press operators. It marked a significant improvement on earlier methods, in which the paper was rubbed by hand to transfer applied ink to the printing surface.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Printing press (easy English)

title: The Age of Enlightenment
brief: Explain the main ideas of the Enlightenment and convince teachers we still need them today.
quirk: Aren't 18th-century ideas outdated in the age of social media?
trick: Aren't 18th-century ideas outdated in the age of social media?
summary: The Age of Enlightenment, also known as the Age of Reason or simply the Enlightenment, was a period of intellectual and cultural flourishing in Europe and Western civilization, emerging in the late 17th century in Western Europe.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Age of Enlightenment (easy English)

title: The Silk Road
brief: Explain what the Silk Road was and convince business people what it teaches us about trade today.
quirk: What can camel caravans teach us about modern trade?
trick: What can camel caravans teach us about modern trade?
summary: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. Spanning over 6,400 km (4,000 mi) on land, it played a central role in facilitating economic, cultural, political, and religious interactions between the Eastern and Western worlds.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Silk Road (easy English)

title: The Scientific Method
brief: Explain how the scientific method works and convince the jury to apply it to everyday decisions.
quirk: Science makes mistakes too — why should we trust it?
trick: Science makes mistakes too — why should we trust it?
summary: The scientific method is an empirical method for acquiring knowledge through careful observation, rigorous skepticism, hypothesis testing, and experimental validation. Developed from ancient and medieval practices, it acknowledges that cognitive assumptions can distort the interpretation of the observation.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Scientific method (easy English)

title: The Prisoner's Dilemma
brief: Explain the prisoner's dilemma and convince business people when cooperating pays off more than competing.
quirk: In real business the tough ones win — why trust competitors?
trick: In real business the tough ones win — why trust competitors?
summary: In game theory, the prisoner's dilemma is a thought experiment involving two rational agents, each of whom can either cooperate for mutual benefit or betray their partner ("defect") for individual gain. The dilemma arises from the fact that while defecting is rational for each agent, cooperation yields a higher payoff for each.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Prisoner's dilemma (easy English)

title: Nash Equilibrium
brief: Explain Nash equilibrium with a real-life example and convince teachers that game theory isn't just for mathematicians.
quirk: People aren't rational — does this work outside the textbook?
trick: People aren't rational — does this work outside the textbook?
summary: In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player could gain more by changing their own strategy in a game. A Nash equilibrium is the most commonly used solution concept for non-cooperative games.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Nash equilibrium (easy English)

title: Gamification
brief: Explain how game mechanics change behavior and convince the jury to use them in learning or work.
quirk: Doesn't it turn everything into chasing points instead of meaning?
trick: Doesn't it turn everything into chasing points instead of meaning?
summary: Gamification is the process of integrating game design elements and principles into non-game contexts in order to increase user engagement and motivation. It is a component of system design.

title: The Butterfly Effect
brief: Explain how small things lead to big consequences and convince people to value small decisions.
quirk: If everything is unpredictable, why plan anything at all?
trick: If everything is unpredictable, why plan anything at all?
summary: In chaos theory, the butterfly effect is the sensitive dependence on initial conditions in which a small change in one state of a deterministic nonlinear system can result in large differences in a later state.

sources.title: Simple English Wikipedia: Butterfly effect (easy English)
